title: NotebookLM (now Gemini Notebook)
readingMarkdown:
# NotebookLM (now Gemini Notebook)

Every assistant in this course so far answers from two places: what it learned in training, and whatever you put in front of it. Most of the time you cannot tell which one an answer came from. **NotebookLM** was built around a different promise. You give it your documents, and it answers from those documents, with a citation on each statement that takes you to the passage it used.

**A note on the name.** In July 2026 Google renamed NotebookLM to **Gemini Notebook**. Google describes the change as one of name and logo, and existing notebooks and links continue to work. Many tutorials, and some of Google's own help pages, still use the old name. This chapter uses "the notebook tool" where the name does not matter.

The idea outlasts the name. This chapter explains what source grounding is and how it is done, what a notebook contains, how to use one for study and research, and where grounding still fails. Details are from Google's pages as of November 2026.

## 1. First-Principles Mental Model & Intuition

### An open-book exam with a strict librarian

Picture an exam in which you may bring any books you like, and a librarian who answers your questions under one rule: every statement must come from the books on the table, and each must be given with the page number.

Ask something the books cover, and you get an answer with page references you can check in seconds. Ask something they do not cover, and the librarian says so.

That is the contract of a source-grounded tool.

```text
   ORDINARY ASSISTANT                        SOURCE-GROUNDED NOTEBOOK

   question                                  question
      |                                         |
      v                                         v
   model's training   +  maybe a search      YOUR SOURCES only
      |                                         |
      v                                         v
   an answer                                 an answer with citations [1] [2]
   (where did this come from?)               (click [1] to see the passage)
                                                |
                                             or: "the sources do not say"
```

Three consequences are worth holding on to.

**The sources are the boundary.** A notebook about your contract knows nothing about contract law in general, and that is the point. Its answers are about your documents.

**Citations make checking cheap.** In Module 3.9 you asked an assistant for quotes so that you could verify them. Here the citation is built in: one click shows the passage.

**The librarian can still misread.** Being limited to the books does not make every reading of them correct. A cited passage can be real and the conclusion drawn from it wrong. Grounding moves the risk from invention to misinterpretation. It does not remove risk.

### A notebook

The unit of work is a **notebook**: a container for one project.

```text
+---------------------------- NOTEBOOK: "Cell biology exam" -----------------------------+
|                                                                                        |
|  SOURCES                    CHAT                          GENERATED OUTPUTS            |
|  lecture-3.pdf              "Where do the light           audio overview               |
|  lecture-4.pdf               reactions occur?"            study guide                  |
|  textbook-ch7.pdf           answer ... [1][2]             flashcards and quiz          |
|  my-notes (Google Doc)                                    mind map                     |
|  a lecture video                                          briefing document            |
|                                                                                        |
+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
     what it may use              asking questions               derived works
```

You add sources, ask questions in the chat, and generate derived works. Everything in the notebook is grounded in the same set of sources, which keeps one project's material from leaking into another's, as with the projects of Module 3.2.

## 2. Core Theory, Mathematical Foundations & Architecture Internals

### How grounding is achieved

Grounding is not a different kind of model. It is the retrieval pipeline of Module 3.2 with two additions: a restriction and a citation.

```text
   ADDING A SOURCE (once)
     document --> extract text --> split into passages --> index

   ASKING A QUESTION (each time)
     question --> find the most relevant passages --+
                                                    v
        instruction: "answer ONLY from these passages, cite each one,
                      and say so if they do not contain the answer"
                                                    |
                                                    v
                                  MODEL --> answer with [passage] markers
```

Two things do the restricting. The retrieval step decides which passages the model sees. The instruction tells the model to stay within them. Neither is a guarantee. Retrieval can miss the right passage. The instruction is text, and as Module 1.10 explained, a model follows instructions with high but not perfect reliability, and it still carries everything it learned in training. A grounded tool is a model strongly steered toward your sources. It is not a model that has forgotten everything else.

### Deciding whether the answer is "in the sources"

The tool has to decide, for each question, whether the retrieved passages are good enough to answer from. Any such decision involves a threshold. Let $s(q, p)$ be a relevance score between the question and the best passage, and $\theta$ the threshold:

$$
\text{response} =
\begin{cases}
\text{answer from } p \text{, with a citation} & \text{if } s(q, p) \ge \theta \\
\text{"not in the sources"} & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$

The threshold trades one error for another.

| Threshold | What goes wrong |
|---|---|
| Too high | **False refusals.** The answer is in the sources, worded differently from the question, and the tool says it is not there |
| Too low | **Unsupported answers.** A loosely related passage is treated as support, and the answer cites something that does not say it |

A real system scores by meaning and is far better than the word counting in this chapter's lab. The trade-off is the same, and it explains two experiences every user of these tools has: being told something is absent when you can see it on the page, and being given a citation that, when clicked, does not quite say what the answer claims.

### What you can put in, and how much

According to Google's help page at the time of writing, limits depend on your plan and are marked as subject to change.

| Plan | Notebooks | Sources per notebook |
|---|---|---|
| Free | 100 | 50 |
| Plus | 200 | 100 |
| Pro | 500 | 300 |
| Ultra | 500 | 500 or more |

A widely quoted figure, which is not on that page, puts the limit for one source at about 500,000 words. Sources have included PDFs, Google Docs, Slides, and Sheets, web pages, pasted text, audio files, images, and videos that have captions.

It is worth doing the arithmetic on those limits. A free notebook filled to capacity could hold

$$
50 \times 500{,}000 = 25{,}000{,}000 \text{ words}
$$

At about 1.33 tokens per word, that is roughly 33 million tokens. Module 3.10 gave the model's context window as about one million. So a full notebook is more than thirty times larger than anything the model can read at once:

$$
\frac{\text{window}}{\text{notebook}} \approx \frac{1{,}000{,}000}{33{,}000{,}000} \approx 3\%
$$

This is the single most useful fact for understanding the tool's behaviour. On a large notebook, any one answer is built from a small selection of passages. A question about a specific point works well, because retrieval can find the few passages that matter. A request to "summarise everything" cannot be satisfied by reading everything, and the result reflects whatever was selected. Module 3.2 made the same point about projects in retrieval mode.

### Sources are copies

When you add a source, the tool works from a copy taken at that moment. An uploaded file is fixed. For a document in Google Drive, the tool has kept a snapshot and has offered a way to re-sync it when the original changes. A notebook can therefore answer correctly from a document that has since been corrected. The citation will be accurate, to the old version.

### Citations, and how to measure them

Each statement in an answer carries numbered markers. Selecting one shows the passage in the source. Citation quality can be measured with two numbers familiar from information retrieval.

**Precision** asks: of the citations given, how many truly support the statement they are attached to?

$$
\text{precision} = \frac{\text{citations that support their claim}}{\text{all citations given}}
$$

**Recall** asks: of the claims made, how many have at least one citation that truly supports them?

$$
\text{recall} = \frac{\text{claims with a valid citation}}{\text{all claims}}
$$

Low precision means clicking a citation often leads somewhere unhelpful. Low recall means claims are floating without real support. A typical failure is the near miss: the citation points to the paragraph next to the one that contains the fact. Technically wrong, usually harmless, and a reminder to read around the cited passage.

### Generated outputs

Beyond chat, the tool turns a notebook's sources into other forms. These have included:

| Output | What it is | Best used for |
|---|---|---|
| **Audio overview** | A spoken discussion of the sources between two AI voices, in several styles and lengths | A first pass through unfamiliar material, away from a screen |
| **Video overview** | Narrated slides generated from the sources | A visual summary |
| **Study guide, briefing document, FAQ, timeline** | Structured written reports | Revision and handing a summary to someone else |
| **Flashcards and quizzes** | Questions generated from the sources | Testing yourself |
| **Mind map** | A branching diagram of topics | Seeing the structure of a subject |
| **Data table** | Information from several sources arranged in rows and columns | Comparison |

Google has also announced that a notebook can be given a computing environment that writes and runs code to analyse data in the sources, starting with its highest plan, and that notebooks can be opened and used from the Gemini app.

Every item in that table is a **derived work**: a new piece of generated content based on the sources. The chat's citations let you check a statement in one click. A two-voice audio discussion has no footnotes. It is the most engaging output and the least checkable, and it compresses hard: a forty-page report becomes ten minutes of conversation. Treat it as an introduction to the material and not as the material.

### Privacy

Google's help pages for the tool state, at the time of writing, that the sources you upload to a personal account are not used to train its models. If you submit feedback on a response, the related content may be reviewed by people. For Workspace and education accounts, the pages state that uploads, questions, and responses are not reviewed by people or used for training. As in Module 3.13, the right account for work material is the work account.

### Where grounding still fails

Grounding lowers the error rate. The evidence says it does not bring it to zero.

- A 2025 study titled "Not Wrong, But Untrue" tested three tools on a reporting task over a collection of 300 documents. About 30 percent of outputs contained at least one hallucination. The general-purpose assistants were at about 40 percent and NotebookLM at about 13 percent. Most errors were not invented facts. They were unsupported characterisations: an opinion attributed to one person in a source restated as a general truth, or an interpretation that went beyond what the documents said.
- A 2024 study from Stanford tested commercial legal research tools that also ground their answers in a document database. It found that they hallucinated on a substantial share of queries, between roughly one in six and one in three depending on the tool.

Two conclusions follow. Grounding helps a great deal: one in eight is much better than two in five. And one in eight is far from never. The characteristic failure of a grounded tool is the confident over-reading: a statement that sounds like the sources and goes a step beyond them.

The mechanical failures are simpler.

| Failure | Cause |
|---|---|
| "Not in the sources", when it is | Wording mismatch, or the passage was not retrieved |
| A citation that does not support the claim | A loosely related passage accepted as support |
| Blended sources | Statements from two documents merged into one claim that neither makes |
| Missing content | Scanned pages without readable text, complex tables, images of text |
| Out-of-date answers | The source changed after it was added |
| Shallow whole-notebook summaries | The notebook is far larger than what can be read at once |

### Complexity

Adding a source costs time proportional to its length, once. Answering costs a search over the passages plus one model call on the few that were selected, which is why a notebook stays responsive as it grows. Checking a citation costs one click, which is the feature's whole value.

## 3. Production-Grade Implementation & Annotated Walkthrough

A miniature of the pipeline shows where each behaviour comes from. First, splitting sources into passages and answering with a citation or a refusal.

```python
STOPWORDS = {"a", "an", "and", "are", "do", "does", "how", "in", "into", "is", "it", "of", "the", "they",
             "to", "what", "where", "who"}

def keywords(text):
    words = {word.strip(".,;:!?()\"'").lower() for word in text.split()}
    return words - STOPWORDS - {""}

SOURCES = {
    "lecture-3.txt": ("Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy. It takes place in the chloroplasts.\n\n"
                      "The light reactions produce ATP and NADPH. They occur in the thylakoid membranes.\n\n"
                      "The Calvin cycle uses ATP and NADPH to fix carbon dioxide into sugar. It occurs in the stroma."),
    "textbook-ch7.txt": ("Cellular respiration releases energy from glucose. It takes place mainly in the mitochondria.\n\n"
                         "Glycolysis splits glucose into pyruvate and occurs in the cytoplasm."),
}

def split_passages(sources):
    passages = []
    for name, text in sources.items():
        paragraphs = [part.strip() for part in text.split("\n\n") if part.strip()]
        for number, paragraph in enumerate(paragraphs, start=1):
            passages.append((f"{name}#{number}", paragraph))
    return passages

def answer(question, passages, threshold=2):
    wanted = keywords(question)
    best_id, best_text, best_score = None, None, 0
    for passage_id, text in passages:
        score = len(wanted & keywords(text))
        if score > best_score:
            best_id, best_text, best_score = passage_id, text, score
    if best_score >= threshold:
        return best_text, best_id
    return "not in sources", None

PASSAGES = split_passages(SOURCES)
for question in ("Where do the light reactions occur?", "What does the Calvin cycle use?",
                 "Who discovered penicillin?", "How is energy released?"):
    print(f"{question:<36} -> {answer(question, PASSAGES)[1]}")
print("with a lower threshold:", answer("How is energy released?", PASSAGES, threshold=1)[1])
```

- **Each passage gets an identifier.** The source's name and the paragraph's number together are the citation. Without an identifier carried from this step, there would be nothing to cite later.
- **`answer` returns the passage and its identifier, or a refusal.** The return value always has the same shape, a text and a citation, with `None` for the citation when the tool declines. Code that calls it must handle the refusal.
- **The first two questions are answered and cited.** They share at least two meaningful words with the right paragraph of the lecture notes.
- **The penicillin question is refused, correctly.** Nothing in the sources mentions it. A general assistant would answer from training. A grounded tool should not.
- **The energy question is refused, wrongly.** The textbook says respiration "releases energy". The question says "released". With word matching, only "energy" is shared, which is below the threshold. This is a false refusal caused by wording.
- **Lowering the threshold makes it worse.** With a threshold of one, the question is answered, from the first paragraph of the lecture notes, which is about photosynthesis and mentions "energy". The tool now gives a confident answer with a citation to the wrong passage. This is the trade-off from Section 2 in five lines of output.

Next, measuring citations.

```python
def citation_scores(claims):
    cited = sum(len(claim["cited"]) for claim in claims)
    correct = sum(len(claim["cited"] & claim["supports"]) for claim in claims)
    supported = sum(1 for claim in claims if claim["cited"] & claim["supports"])
    precision = correct / cited if cited else 0.0
    recall = supported / len(claims) if claims else 0.0
    return precision, recall

REVIEW = [
    {"cited": {"lecture-3.txt#2"}, "supports": {"lecture-3.txt#2"}},
    {"cited": {"lecture-3.txt#3", "textbook-ch7.txt#1"}, "supports": {"lecture-3.txt#3"}},
    {"cited": {"lecture-3.txt#1"}, "supports": {"lecture-3.txt#2"}},
    {"cited": set(), "supports": {"textbook-ch7.txt#2"}},
]
print(citation_scores(REVIEW))
```

- **Each reviewed claim records two sets.** The passages the answer cited, and the passages a person judged to support the claim. Someone has to do that judging. The scores summarise a review, and do not replace it.
- **Precision counts citations.** Four citations were given across the claims and two of them are right, so precision is 0.5.
- **Recall counts claims.** Two of the four claims have a citation that truly supports them. The third cites the neighbouring paragraph, and the fourth has no citation at all.
- **The third claim is the near miss.** The right passage is next to the cited one. In practice this is the reason to read the paragraph above and below a citation before deciding the answer is wrong.

Then, capacity and stale sources.

```python
import hashlib

def capacity_check(word_counts, max_sources=50, max_words=500_000):
    problems = []
    if len(word_counts) > max_sources:
        problems.append("too-many-sources")
    problems.extend(f"too-long: {name}" for name, words in word_counts.items() if words > max_words)
    return problems

def fingerprint(text):
    return hashlib.sha256(text.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()[:12]

def stale_sources(synced, current):
    return sorted(name for name, mark in synced.items() if name not in current or fingerprint(current[name]) != mark)

print(capacity_check({"thesis.pdf": 82_000, "archive.pdf": 640_000}))
print(f"a full free notebook: {50 * 500_000:,} words, about {50 * 500_000 * 1.33 / 1e6:.0f} million tokens, "
      f"of which a 1M window is {1_000_000 / (50 * 500_000 * 1.33):.0%}")

synced = {name: fingerprint(text) for name, text in SOURCES.items()}
edited = dict(SOURCES)
edited["lecture-3.txt"] = SOURCES["lecture-3.txt"].replace("thylakoid membranes", "thylakoid membranes of the chloroplast")
print(stale_sources(synced, edited))
```

- **Limits are parameters.** The documented limits differ by plan and are marked as subject to change. The function takes them as arguments with the free plan's values as defaults.
- **Every problem is listed.** Too many sources is reported once. Each over-long source is named, so that you know which document to split.
- **The capacity line is the arithmetic from Section 2.** Twenty-five million words is about 33 million tokens, of which a one-million-token window is about 3 percent.
- **A fingerprint records what the notebook copied.** `synced` holds a short code for each source at the moment it was added. The original lecture file is then edited.
- **`stale_sources` finds the difference.** The lecture notes' current fingerprint no longer matches, so the notebook is answering from an old copy. A source that has been deleted from the original location is reported too. The tool's citations would still look perfectly valid.

**Complexity.** `split_passages` is linear in the size of the sources. `answer` is linear in the number of passages. `citation_scores` is linear in the number of claims. `stale_sources` is linear in the total size of the current sources.

### Workflows that work

**Studying a subject.**

```text
1. One notebook per course unit. Add the lecture notes, the chapter, your own notes.
2. Ask for a study guide. Read it against the sources and fix what it got wrong.
3. Listen to an audio overview once, as an introduction.
4. Use the quiz and flashcards. For every answer you get wrong, click the citation and
   read the passage, not the summary.
5. Ask "what do my sources NOT cover from this syllabus?" and paste the syllabus.
```

**Working through a long report.**

```text
1. Add the report and any related documents.
2. Ask specific questions: "What does section 4 say about liability?"
3. Click every citation behind anything you will repeat.
4. For a whole-document view, ask section by section and assemble the result yourself.
```

**Comparing sources.**

```text
1. Add the documents to be compared, clearly named.
2. Ask for a table: "For each source, what does it say about X? Leave a cell blank
   where a source says nothing."
3. Check each cell's citation. Blended statements show up here first.
```

In each workflow the tool finds and organises, and you read the passages that matter.

## 4. Practitioner Wisdom & Edge Cases (Reddit / HN / Stack Overflow Synthesis)

Much of what is written about this tool is enthusiastic, and the recurring cautions come from the published studies and from users' reports.

**Audio overviews embellish.** The two-voice discussions are the feature people love most. Users also report that the hosts overstate findings, add framing that is not in the sources, and flatten qualifications. Enjoy the overview, and do not quote it.

**A citation is not proof.** The study described in Section 2 found that the commonest error in grounded answers was over-reading: stating more than the cited passage supports. Click through for anything you will repeat, and read the sentence in its paragraph.

**"It is not in your sources", when it is.** Rephrase the question in the document's own words, or name the source. As with projects in Module 3.2, a wording mismatch is the usual cause.

**"Summarise all my sources" disappoints on big notebooks.** A notebook can hold far more than the model reads at once. Ask about one source at a time, or one topic, and combine the answers.

**Blended sources.** Asked a question that two documents answer differently, the tool may merge them into a statement neither makes. When sources might disagree, ask for each one's position separately.

**Scanned and visual material.** A scanned PDF with no readable text layer, a table laid out in an unusual way, or text inside an image may be partly or wholly missed, without an error. Test each new source with a question whose answer you know.

**Videos need captions.** A video without captions may not work as a source, because there is no text to index.

**Stale copies.** A Google Doc you edited yesterday is not automatically what the notebook is reading. Re-sync after changes, and be aware that an uploaded file never updates.

**The source is wrong.** Grounding guarantees fidelity to your documents and nothing about their truth. A notebook built on an outdated textbook or a biased report will give you outdated or biased answers with impeccable citations.

**It is not a general assistant.** People ask a notebook for general knowledge and are frustrated by refusals, or, worse, receive an answer that draws on training without making that clear. Use the notebook for what is in the sources and a general assistant for everything else.

**Limits and names keep changing.** Daily limits on chats and audio generations have been revised more than once, and the product has been renamed. Check the current help page before planning heavy use.

**Personal and work accounts differ.** The data-handling terms differ, and feedback submitted from a personal account can be reviewed by people. Put work documents in the work account's notebook.

## 5. Active Recall Check & Synthesis Summary

**Summary.** The notebook tool, launched as NotebookLM and renamed Gemini Notebook in 2026, answers from the sources you add to a notebook and cites the passage behind each statement. Grounding is retrieval plus an instruction to stay within what was retrieved, so it strongly steers the model without guaranteeing anything. A threshold decides whether the sources contain an answer, trading false refusals against unsupported answers. A notebook can hold far more than the model reads at once, about thirty times more at the free limits, so specific questions work better than whole-notebook requests. Sources are copies and can go stale. Citation quality is measured by precision and recall, and the typical failure is a real passage over-read. Studies put the error rate of grounded tools well below that of general assistants and well above zero. Generated outputs such as audio overviews are derived works with no footnotes. The habit that makes the tool reliable is the one it makes cheap: click the citation.

**Question 1.** A Pro-plan notebook holds 300 sources averaging 120,000 words each. Estimate its size in tokens at 1.33 tokens per word, and the fraction a one-million-token context window represents. What does this imply for the request "write a summary of everything in this notebook", and how should the user proceed?

<details>
<summary>View Answer</summary>

Three hundred sources of 120,000 words is 36,000,000 words. At 1.33 tokens per word that is about 47,900,000 tokens. A one-million-token window is about 2 percent of that. So at most a fiftieth of the notebook can be in front of the model at any moment, and in practice less, since the answer and the instructions need room. A request to summarise everything therefore cannot be met by reading everything. The tool retrieves a selection of passages it judges relevant to the word "summary" and the general topic, and writes from those. The result will read like a summary and will reflect the selection, with no indication of the forty-nine fiftieths that were not consulted. The user should break the task into pieces that retrieval can serve well. Ask about one source at a time, or one topic at a time across sources: "What does the 2024 audit say about procurement?" Collect those answers, each with its citations, and assemble the overall summary, either by hand or by asking the tool to combine the pieces. Where a complete reading of one long source is needed, a tool that loads the whole document, as in Module 3.9, is the better choice.

</details>

**Question 2.** A reviewer checks an answer containing five claims. Claim A has one citation, which supports it. Claim B has two citations, of which one supports it. Claim C has one citation, to a passage that does not support it. Claim D has no citation. Claim E has three citations, all supporting. Compute citation precision and recall, and say what each number tells the user.

<details>
<summary>View Answer</summary>

The citations given number one, two, one, zero, and three, a total of seven. Of these, the supporting ones are one for A, one for B, none for C, none for D, and three for E, a total of five. Precision is 5 out of 7, about 0.71. For recall, a claim counts if it has at least one citation that truly supports it: A, B, and E do, C and D do not, so recall is 3 out of 5, or 0.6. Precision tells the user how much to trust a click: about seven times in ten, following a citation leads to a passage that really supports the statement, and three times in ten it does not. Recall tells the user how much of the answer is actually held up by the sources: two of the five claims have no valid support, one because its citation is wrong and one because it has none. The two numbers point to different remedies. Low precision means reading each cited passage before relying on it. Low recall means treating uncited or wrongly cited claims as unverified and asking the tool specifically where each came from. A claim with no citation in a tool designed to cite everything is a particular warning, since it may have come from the model's general knowledge.

</details>

**Question 3.** A student builds a notebook from last year's edition of a textbook and a classmate's notes, listens to the audio overview twice, and writes an essay from memory of it. The essay contains an outdated figure, a claim the textbook presents as one researcher's view stated as established fact, and a detail that appears in neither source. Trace each error to a property of the tool described in this chapter, and describe a better process.

<details>
<summary>View Answer</summary>

The outdated figure comes from the sources themselves. Grounding makes answers faithful to the documents supplied and says nothing about whether those documents are current. Last year's edition produces last year's figure, accurately cited. The opinion stated as fact is the over-reading that the published study found to be the commonest error in grounded tools: a view attributed to one person in the source is restated as a general truth. It is especially likely in an audio overview, which compresses and dramatises, and has no citations through which the student could have caught it. The detail that appears in neither source is either an embellishment in the audio overview, which users report, or the model drawing on its training despite the instruction to stay within the sources, since grounding steers the model and does not erase what it knows. Writing from memory of an audio discussion then removed every remaining chance of checking. A better process starts with current sources: the latest edition, and the lecture notes. The audio overview is used once, as an introduction. The student then asks specific questions in the chat, clicks the citation behind every fact intended for the essay, and reads the passage in context to see whether it is stated as fact or as someone's view. Figures are checked against the current edition. The essay is written with the sources open.

</details>

interactiveLab.labTitle: Hands-On Lab: A Grounded Question-Answering Simulator with Citations
interactiveLab.context: A study group is preparing for an exam from lecture notes and a textbook chapter and wants to understand why a source-grounded tool sometimes refuses, sometimes cites the wrong passage, and sometimes works from an old copy. You will build a miniature of such a tool: a passage splitter, an answerer that cites or declines, a scorer for citation quality, a capacity check, and a detector for sources that have changed since they were added.
interactiveLab.starterCode:
"""
Lab: A Grounded Question-Answering Simulator with Citations
Standard library only. Complete the TODO in each step, then press "Run & Verify Step".
"""
import hashlib

STOPWORDS = {"a", "an", "and", "are", "do", "does", "how", "in", "into", "is", "it", "of", "the", "they",
             "to", "what", "where", "who"}

SOURCES = {
    "lecture-3.txt": ("Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy. It takes place in the chloroplasts.\n\n"
                      "The light reactions produce ATP and NADPH. They occur in the thylakoid membranes.\n\n"

"""
Lab solution: A Grounded Question-Answering Simulator with Citations
Standard library only.
"""
import hashlib

STOPWORDS = {"a", "an", "and", "are", "do", "does", "how", "in", "into", "is", "it", "of", "the", "they",
             "to", "what", "where", "who"}

SOURCES = {
    "lecture-3.txt": ("Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy. It takes place in the chloroplasts.\n\n"
                      "The light reactions produce ATP and NADPH. They occur in the thylakoid membranes.\n\n"
                      "The Calvin cycle uses ATP and NADPH to fix carbon dioxide into sugar. It occurs in the stroma."),
    "textbook-ch7.txt": ("Cellular respiration releases energy from glucose. It takes place mainly in the mitochondria.\n\n"
                         "Glycolysis splits glucose into pyruvate and occurs in the cytoplasm."),
}

REVIEW = [
    {"cited": {"lecture-3.txt#2"}, "supports": {"lecture-3.txt#2"}},
    {"cited": {"lecture-3.txt#3", "textbook-ch7.txt#1"}, "supports": {"lecture-3.txt#3"}},
    {"cited": {"lecture-3.txt#1"}, "supports": {"lecture-3.txt#2"}},
    {"cited": set(), "supports": {"textbook-ch7.txt#2"}},
]


def keywords(text):
    """Provided helper: the set of meaningful lowercase words in a text."""
    words = {word.strip(".,;:!?()\"'").lower() for word in text.split()}
    return words - STOPWORDS - {""}


def fingerprint(text):
    """Provided helper: a short code that changes whenever the text changes."""
    return hashlib.sha256(text.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()[:12]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 1
def split_passages(sources):
    """Every passage carries an identifier from this step on. Without it there would be
    nothing to cite later."""
    passages = []
    for name, text in sources.items():
        paragraphs = [part.strip() for part in text.split("\n\n") if part.strip()]
        for number, paragraph in enumerate(paragraphs, start=1):
            passages.append((f"{name}#{number}", paragraph))
    return passages


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 2
def answer(question, passages, threshold=2):
    """The threshold trades false refusals (too high) against unsupported answers (too low).
    A real system scores by meaning, and the trade-off is the same."""
    wanted = keywords(question)
    best_id, best_text, best_score = None, None, 0
    for passage_id, text in passages:
        score = len(wanted & keywords(text))
        if score > best_score:
            best_id, best_text, best_score = passage_id, text, score
    if best_score >= threshold:
        return best_text, best_id
    return "not in sources", None


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 3
def citation_scores(claims):
    """Precision counts citations; recall counts claims. The 'supports' sets come from a
    person's judgement: the scores summarise a review and do not replace it."""
    cited = sum(len(claim["cited"]) for claim in claims)
    correct = sum(len(claim["cited"] & claim["supports"]) for claim in claims)
    supported = sum(1 for claim in claims if claim["cited"] & claim["supports"])
    precision = correct / cited if cited else 0.0
    recall = supported / len(claims) if claims else 0.0
    return precision, recall


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 4
def capacity_check(word_counts, max_sources=50, max_words=500_000):
    """Limits differ by plan and change, so they are arguments. Every problem is listed."""
    problems = []
    if len(word_counts) > max_sources:
        problems.append("too-many-sources")
    problems.extend(f"too-long: {name}" for name, words in word_counts.items() if words > max_words)
    return problems


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 5
def stale_sources(synced, current):
    """A notebook works from copies. Its citations to an old copy look perfectly valid."""
    return sorted(name for name, mark in synced.items() if name not in current or fingerprint(current[name]) != mark)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    passages = split_passages(SOURCES)
    for question in ("Where do the light reactions occur?", "What does the Calvin cycle use?",
                     "Who discovered penicillin?", "How is energy released?"):
        print(f"{question:<36} -> {answer(question, passages)[1]}")
    print("with a lower threshold:", answer("How is energy released?", passages, threshold=1)[1])

    print(citation_scores(REVIEW))

    print(capacity_check({"thesis.pdf": 82_000, "archive.pdf": 640_000}))
    print(f"a full free notebook: {50 * 500_000:,} words, about {50 * 500_000 * 1.33 / 1e6:.0f} million tokens, "
          f"of which a 1M window is {1_000_000 / (50 * 500_000 * 1.33):.0%}")

    synced = {name: fingerprint(text) for name, text in SOURCES.items()}
    edited = dict(SOURCES)
    edited["lecture-3.txt"] = SOURCES["lecture-3.txt"].replace("thylakoid membranes", "thylakoid membranes of the chloroplast")
    print(stale_sources(synced, edited))
    print(f"recall question 1: {300 * 120_000 * 1.33:,.0f} tokens, window share {1_000_000 / (300 * 120_000 * 1.33):.1%}")
    print("recall question 2:", 5 / 7, 3 / 5)
